topics.title: The 把 construction
topics.description: Putting the object first to talk about what you do TO it

guide.intro: 把 (bǎ) is one of the most distinctive features of Mandarin grammar. It moves the object before the verb to say "take X and do something to it". You'll hear it constantly — and English doesn't have a clean equivalent.

sections.text: The basic shape

Normal Chinese order is Subject–Verb–Object. With 把, you reorder to Subject–把–Object–Verb–(extra). The "extra" part is crucial — 把 sentences almost never end on a bare verb. There has to be a result, location, or change attached.

rows: 我 把 门 关 上
他 把 苹果 吃 了
请 放 书 在 桌子 上
请 把 书 放 在 桌子 上

sections.text: When to use 把
Use 把 when you want to emphasize what HAPPENS TO a specific, known object — moving it, finishing it, changing it, putting it somewhere. Both speaker and listener know which object you mean.

rows.source: 我 把 作业 做 完 了。
rows.pinyin: Wǒ bǎ zuòyè zuò wán le.

rows.source: 请 把 窗户 打 开。
他 把 杯子 打 破 了。
rows.pinyin: Tā bǎ bēizi dǎ pò le.

sections.text: If you can't say what HAPPENS TO the object, don't use 把. "我 把 苹果 喜欢" is wrong — 喜欢 (like) doesn't change the apple.
What can't follow 把
把 needs a verb that physically affects the object. Verbs that don't qualify: feeling/perception verbs (爱, 喜欢, 觉得, 知道), existence verbs (有, 是), and most stative or motion-only verbs (来, 去, 走).

rows.source: 我 喜欢 这 本 书。
rows.translation: I like this book. (NOT 我 把 这 本 书 喜欢)

rows.source: 他 知道 答案。
rows.translation: He knows the answer. (NOT 他 把 答案 知道)

sections.text: Negation: 没 / 不 goes BEFORE 把

rows.source: 我 没 把 作业 做 完。
rows.pinyin: Wǒ méi bǎ zuòyè zuò wán.

rows.source: 请 不要 把 门 关 上。
rows.pinyin: Qǐng bú yào bǎ mén guān shàng.

lessons.title: Why object-fronting?
lessons.description: Transform plain SVO into S 把 O V

exercises.prompt: Rewrite "我 关 门" with 把 — "I closed the door"
exercises.answer: 我 把 门 关 上 了
exercises.explanation: Take the object 门, move it after 把, and add a result (上) and 了 to complete the action.

exercises.prompt: Rewrite "他 喝 了 咖啡" with 把 — "He drank up the coffee"
exercises.answer: 他 把 咖啡 喝 完 了
exercises.explanation: Move 咖啡 to the 把 slot. Add 完 (finished) so the verb has a result.

exercises.prompt: Rewrite "请 放 书 在 桌子 上" with 把 — "Please put the book on the table"
exercises.answer: 请 把 书 放 在 桌子 上
exercises.explanation: Object-fronting is the rule whenever you tell someone WHERE to put something. The location 在 桌子 上 lives where the result usually goes.

exercises.prompt: Why use 把 instead of plain SVO?
options: To emphasize WHAT HAPPENS to a known specific object
exercises.answer: To emphasize WHAT HAPPENS to a known specific object

exercises.prompt: Rewrite "我 写 完 信 了" with 把 — "I finished writing the letter"
exercises.answer: 我 把 信 写 完 了

exercises.prompt: Match plain to 把-version

pairs.right: 我 把 灯 关 了
他 把 饭 吃 完 了
我 把 衣服 洗 好 了
她 把 窗户 打 开 了

exercises.prompt: "我 ___ 钥匙 找 到 了" — fill the missing word
exercises.answer: 把

exercises.prompt: What's wrong with "我 把 苹果 喜欢"?
options: 喜欢 doesn't change the apple — 把 needs an action that affects the object
exercises.answer: 喜欢 doesn't change the apple — 把 needs an action that affects the object
exercises.explanation: 把 needs disposal — the object must be physically/conceptually changed by the verb. 喜欢 (like) doesn't change anything.

exercises.prompt: Pick the right 把-version: "I drank up that cup of tea"
options: 我 把 那 杯 茶 喝 完 了
我 把 喝 那 杯 茶 完 了
那 杯 茶 我 把 喝 完 了
我 喝 把 那 杯 茶 完 了
exercises.answer: 我 把 那 杯 茶 喝 完 了
exercises.explanation: When you 把 something, add a result like 完 / 光 / 好 — "finished/all gone/done".

exercises.prompt: What's the function of 把 in "我 把 门 关 上"?
options: Moves the object before the verb to focus on what happens to it
exercises.answer: Moves the object before the verb to focus on what happens to it

lessons.title: When 把 needs a result
lessons.description: Why bare verbs don't work after 把

exercises.prompt: Which sentence is the most natural?
options: 我 把 苹果 吃
我 把 苹果 吃 完 了
我 苹果 把 吃
exercises.answer: 我 把 苹果 吃 完 了
exercises.explanation: 把 sentences need something after the verb. A bare 了 (我 把 苹果 吃 了) works but a result complement like 完 (finished) or 光 (all gone) is more natural and specific.

exercises.prompt: Build "He broke the cup"
exercises.answer: 他 把 杯子 打 破 了

exercises.prompt: Build "I lost the key" with 把
exercises.answer: 我 把 钥匙 丢 了
exercises.explanation: 丢 (to lose) carries its own "gone" result so a bare 了 is enough — no extra complement needed.

exercises.prompt: Match the verb to its result complement
Pick the only INCORRECT 把 sentence:
options: 我 把 灯 关 了
我 把 房间 打扫 干净 了
我 把 字 写 错 了
exercises.answer: 我 把 作业

topics.title: The 被 passive
topics.description: When something happens TO the subject — usually unpleasantly

guide.intro: 被 (bèi) is the passive marker — "got / was done by". It's the mirror image of 把: where 把 puts the actor first and the patient mid-sentence, 被 puts the patient (victim) first.

sections.text: The basic shape
Pattern: Patient + 被 + (Agent) + Verb + result. The agent is optional — drop it if it's unknown or obvious.

rows.source: 我 的 手机 被 偷 了。
rows.pinyin: Wǒ de shǒujī bèi tōu le.

rows.source: 杯子 被 他 打 破 了。
rows.pinyin: Bēizi bèi tā dǎ pò le.
rows.translation: The cup was broken by him.

rows.source: 钱 被 老板 拿走 了。
rows.pinyin: Qián bèi lǎobǎn ná zǒu le.
rows.translation: The money was taken by the boss.

sections.text: 把 vs 被 — same event, different POV

rows: 他 把 杯子 打 破 了
杯子 被 他 打 破 了
小偷 偷 了 我 的 手机
我 的 手机 被 (小偷) 偷 了

sections.text: Mandarin's 被 has a slightly negative or unfortunate flavor — it's used much more often for bad things (got stolen, broken, scolded) than for neutral or good ones. Sentences like "I was praised" (我 被 表扬 了) work but feel marked.
叫 / 让 — informal alternatives
In speech, 叫 (jiào) or 让 (ràng) often replace 被. They sound more casual — but unlike 被, they REQUIRE an agent.

rows.source: 我 的 钱 让 他 拿走 了。
rows.pinyin: Wǒ de qián ràng tā ná zǒu le.
rows.translation: My money got taken by him.

rows.source: 他 叫 老师 批评 了。
rows.translation: He got scolded by the teacher.

sections.text: Negation
Same as 把 — put 没 BEFORE 被.

rows.source: 我 的 手机 没 被 偷。
rows.pinyin: Wǒ de shǒujī méi bèi tōu.

sections.text: Two flavors of 了
Mandarin uses 了 in two distinct slots, and 把 / 被 sentences often need both. Knowing which is which is the difference between a complete sentence and a fragment.

rows: Something is now different / new situation

rows.source: 他 吃 了 三 个 苹果。
rows.pinyin: Tā chī le sān ge píngguǒ.
rows.translation: He ate three apples. (perfective 了₁ — action complete)

rows.source: 下 雨 了。
rows.translation: It's raining now. (sentence 了₂ — change of state, didn't use to be)

rows.source: 已经 下 了 三 天 雨 了。
rows.pinyin: Yǐjīng xià le sān tiān yǔ le.
rows.translation: It's been raining for three days. (BOTH 了 — completed duration AND ongoing relevance)

sections.text: Quick test: if the 了 hugs the verb (verb 了 object), it's 了₁. If the 了 is at the very end of the sentence, it's 了₂. Same character, different jobs.

topics.title: Giving with 给
topics.description: 给 as both "give" and a coverb meaning "for / to"

guide.intro: 给 (gěi) wears two hats. As a main verb it means "give". As a coverb sitting before another verb, it marks the recipient or beneficiary — "for someone", "to someone". Both uses are everywhere.

sections.text: 给 as main verb — "give"
Pattern: Subject + 给 + recipient + thing. Two objects in a row, recipient first.

rows.source: 我 给 他 一 本 书。
rows.pinyin: Wǒ gěi tā yì běn shū.

rows.source: 妈妈 给 我 钱。

sections.text: 给 as coverb — "for / to"
Sandwiched before another verb, 给 marks who benefits or receives the action. Pattern: Subject + 给 + recipient + verb + object.

rows.source: 我 给 你 买 了 一 杯 咖啡。
rows.pinyin: Wǒ gěi nǐ mǎi le yì bēi kāfēi.
rows.translation: I bought you a coffee. (the buying is FOR you)

rows.source: 他 给 妈妈 打 电话。
rows.translation: He's calling mom. (the call is TO mom)

rows.source: 请 给 我 介绍 一下。

sections.text: Notice how 给 you 买 (buy for you) and 给 妈妈 打 电话 (call mom) both keep 给 + person BEFORE the main verb. English flips this around — Chinese is rigid about the order.

topics.title: How well? — 得 complement
topics.description: Modify a verb with how it was done — 得 + adjective

guide.intro: 得 (de) lets you describe the manner or degree of an action: not WHAT you did, but HOW WELL or HOW MUCH. It's the closest Mandarin gets to English adverbs.

sections.text: The basic pattern
Pattern: Subject + Verb + 得 + (very) + Adjective. Note the position of 很 — almost always required to keep the sentence sounding natural.

rows.source: 他 跑 得 很 快。
她 唱 得 很 好。
我 睡 得 不 好。

sections.text: When the verb has an object
If your verb takes an object, you have to repeat the verb. Mandarin can't have an object AND a 得 phrase on the same verb. Pattern: Subject + Verb + Object, Verb + 得 + adjective.

rows.source: 他 说 中文 说 得 很 好。
rows.pinyin: Tā shuō Zhōngwén shuō de hěn hǎo.
rows.translation: He speaks Chinese very well. (literally: "speaks Chinese, speaks very well")

rows.source: 她 写 字 写 得 很 漂亮。
rows.pinyin: Tā xiě zì xiě de hěn piàoliang.

sections.text: Common mistake: "他 说 中文 得 很 好" — wrong. The verb has to repeat. Or you can drop the object: "他 中文 说 得 很 好" also works.
Three different 得 / 的 / 地

rows: after a verb: how it was done
走 得 慢 — walks slowly

sections.text: All three are pronounced "de" (neutral tone) — only writing distinguishes them. Pay attention to position: 的 between nouns, 地 before verbs, 得 after verbs.
Negation: not 不 before 得 — 不 before the adjective

topics.title: Opinions & agreement
topics.description: I think, I believe, I agree — saying what you reckon

guide.intro: B1 means saying more than "I like" or "I want". You need ways to express opinions softly, agree, disagree, and ask people what THEY think. Three verbs do the heavy lifting: 觉得, 认为, and 看.

sections.text: 觉得 — feel / think (everyday)
觉得 (jué de) is the workhorse — "I feel / think that...". Use it for any soft, personal opinion. By far the most common in conversation.

rows.source: 我 觉得 这 个 电影 很 好。
rows.pinyin: Wǒ juéde zhè ge diànyǐng hěn hǎo.
rows.translation: I think this movie is good.

rows.source: 你 觉得 怎么样？

sections.text: 认为 — believe / hold (more formal)
认为 (rèn wéi) is firmer and more written — "I hold the view that...". Right for opinions on bigger issues, news, business, debate.

rows.source: 我 认为 这 个 计划 不 行。
rows.pinyin: Wǒ rènwéi zhè ge jìhuà bù xíng.
rows.translation: I don't think this plan will work.

rows.source: 专家 认为 经济 会 好转。
rows.translation: Experts believe the economy will improve.

sections.text: 看 — see / view (informal opinion ask)
看 (kàn) literally means "look", but "你 看 …" idiomatically means "in your view, …". Used to gently ask someone's take.

rows.source: 你 看 我 该 怎么 办？
rows.pinyin: Nǐ kàn wǒ gāi zěnme bàn?
rows.translation: What do you think I should do?

rows.source: 我 看 应该 没 问题。
rows.translation: I think it should be fine.

sections.text: Agreeing & disagreeing
Chinese conversation tends to soften disagreement. "我 不 太 同意" (I don't really agree) is gentler and more common than a flat "不 同意".

topics.title: Telling a story
topics.description: Sequencing past events with 着 and directional verbs

guide.intro: When you narrate a story you need ways to set the scene ("she was sitting"), describe motion ("he walked in"), and string events together. 着 handles ongoing states; directional complements like 上来 and 下去 handle motion in space.

sections.text: 着 — ongoing state
着 (zhe) attached to a verb means "in the state of doing". It's NOT the same as English -ing — 着 emphasizes a held position or background condition, often setting the scene.

rows.source: 他 站 着。
rows.translation: He is standing. (in a standing state)

rows.source: 门 开 着。
她 笑 着 说。

sections.text: 着 vs 在: 在 means "actively doing right now" ("我 在 吃饭" — I'm eating). 着 means "in this state" ("门 开 着" — the door's open). For narration, 着 sets the scene; 在 reports a live action.
Directional complements: 上 / 下 / 进 / 出 / 来 / 去
Six little words combine into rich verbs of motion. Pair a base direction (up/down/in/out) with 来 (toward speaker) or 去 (away from speaker).

rows.source: 他 走 进来 了。
她 跑 出去 了。
请 上来。

sections.text: Figurative directionals — 起来 / 下去 / 出来
Directional complements stretch beyond physical motion. Attached to non-motion verbs, they signal phase or aspect: starting, continuing, or coming-to-clarity.

rows: 看 起来 很 累 — looks tired

rows.source: 我 终于 想 出来 了。
请 你 说 下 去。
他 突然 笑 起来 了。

sections.text: Sequencing words
A2's 然后 still works, but B1 stories add 先...再... (first...then...), 最后 (finally), 突然 (suddenly), and 后来 (afterward — for events further apart).

rows.pinyin: Wǒ xiān chīfàn, zài kàn diànyǐng.
rows.translation: First I'll eat, then watch a movie.

rows.source: 突然 下雨 了。
后来 他 搬 走 了。
